About this simulation

Physics

A localized Gaussian wavepacket propagates toward a symmetric rectangular barrier with V(x) = U for |x| < a. The model is one-dimensional, non-relativistic, spinless quantum mechanics (free-electron mass). Depending on energy and barrier geometry, the packet partially reflects and partially transmits; for E < U, the transmitted component is quantum tunneling.

Simulation visuals

The top panel shows the barrier profile and carrier-energy reference. The lower panel shows Re(ψ), Im(ψ), and |ψ|² versus position, including packet spreading and barrier interaction. Absorbing layers at both boundaries suppress wrap-around reflections from the FFT domain and support cleaner reflection/transmission estimates.

Controls

Use sliders to tune U, a, carrier E, packet width σ, initial center x₀, and playback speed. Toggle Re(ψ), Im(ψ), and |ψ|² traces; the regime badge compares carrier E to U, while Wavepacket Info reports broader packet-energy context.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The barrier

Here’s our setup. A Gaussian wavepacket — an electron spread over a few nanometres — travels toward a rectangular barrier of height U and width 2a. The top panel shows you the barrier and the packet’s carrier energy E; the lower panel shows ψ and |ψ|². Right now E = 0.20 eV and U = 0.30 eV, so the barrier stands taller than the packet’s energy.

2 · The classical particle

Let’s start with classical physics. A particle with kinetic energy 0.20 eV heads toward a barrier that takes 0.30 eV to cross. What do you think happens when it arrives?

3 · The quantum packet

Now for the quantum version. The wavepacket approaches the same barrier — E = 0.20 eV against U = 0.30 eV. When it arrives, what do you expect to happen to |ψ|²?

4 · The transmitted packet

Let’s watch that again — the run repeats. Compare the small transmitted packet with the incident one. How do you think it travels on the far side of the barrier?

5 · A wider barrier

Now let’s make the barrier thicker. The barrier half-width doubles, a = 0.50 nm → 1.00 nm, and everything else stays fixed. What’s your guess? The transmitted fraction…

6 · Above the barrier

One last experiment. The carrier energy is raised to E = 0.60 eV — twice the barrier height — so classically every particle now crosses. But what about the wave? The quantum packet…

The Physics

Quantum tunneling · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim launches a quantum wave packet, with the mass of an electron, at a rectangular barrier and reports how much of it ends up on each side. It is the simplest model of an electron meeting a thin insulating layer or a gap between two surfaces.

What you'll learn

  • How the barrier's height U and thickness, and the packet's energy E, decide the share on each side.
  • What Re ψ, Im ψ and |ψ|² each show, and how they differ.
  • How the textbook T relates to what a real packet does.
  • What changes when E is below, at or above U.
The sim at t = 0, default settings: the barrier and the energy E (top), Re ψ with |ψ|² shaded (bottom).

What's on screen

  • Barrier V(x) (red, top panel): height U, thickness 2a.
  • Carrier E (dashed cyan): the packet's central energy.
  • Re ψ (blue, bottom panel): the real part of the wave function.
  • Im ψ (amber): the imaginary part.
  • |ψ|² (purple): the probability density. The shaded band marks the barrier.
  • Outcome bar: Reflection and Transmission estimates, "— %" until the packet has met the barrier.
  • Wavepacket Info and Physics (sidebar): the packet's numbers, and the plane-wave T.
See itLaunch the default packet at 3× speed. Watch for: the packet reaching the barrier, then the Reflection and Transmission estimates replacing "— %" after about 7 s.

03

The packet and the barrier

The sim evolves ψ(x, t) with the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, in one dimension, for a particle of electron mass:

The barrier is V = U for |x| ≤ a and 0 elsewhere.

At t = 0 the packet is a Gaussian of width σ centered at x₀, moving right with wave number k₀:

The initial state, as the sim builds it.
  • E = ħ²k₀²/2m is the packet's central energy (the dashed line). Its speed is vg = ħk₀/m.
  • A packet confined to a width σ is a sum of many wave numbers, spread by 1/(2σ). Its energy spread is ΔE = ħvg/2σ: 58 meV at the defaults.
  • A narrower packet has a wider ΔE. The sim flags k₀σ as "(low)" below 3: the packet is then too narrow for one energy to describe it well.
  • The plane-wave formulas in the Physics panel are for a single energy. Section 07 returns to the difference.
See itNarrow the packet to σ = 0.50 nm. Watch for: ΔE in Wavepacket Info rising from 58 to about 175 meV, with k₀σ flagged "(low)".
04

Inside the barrier

Where E < U, the Schrödinger equation gives real exponentials instead of sines. The wave does not end at the wall: it decays.

κ = √(2m(U − E))/ħ; the decay length is 1/κ.
  • At the defaults, 1/κ = 0.617 nm (Wavepacket Info prints it) and the barrier is 2a = 1.0 nm thick: 1.6 decay lengths.
  • If any wave is left at the far face, V = 0 again, so it carries on as an ordinary traveling wave with the same k: the same wavelength and speed, but a smaller amplitude.
  • The barrier removes amplitude, not energy.
The steady-state wave at the defaults: ripples on the left, decay in the barrier, a smaller steady wave on the right (|t|² = T = 13.1%).
See itRun the default packet and freeze it at t = 24 fs. Watch for: the purple |ψ|² reaching into the shaded band and thinning across it, with a low tail already beyond the far wall.
05

Thickness and height set T

Matching ψ and its slope at both faces gives the exact plane-wave T that the Physics panel evaluates:

Exact, for E < U.

Across the thickness 2a the amplitude falls by about e−2κa, so the probability falls by about e−4κa:

The thick-barrier form. At the defaults (2κa = 1.6) it gives 13.9%, against the exact 13.10%.

κ is inside the exponent, so T is steep in both a and U − E:

06

Above the barrier, some still reflects

For E > U the wave oscillates inside the barrier, with a different wave number k₂ = √(2m(E − U))/ħ. A change in wave number reflects part of a wave, so the two faces still reflect.

Exact, for E > U.
  • At E = 0.60 eV, U = 0.30 eV, a = 0.50 nm the plane-wave formula gives T = 98.66%, so R = 1.34%.
  • The two reflections interfere. T = 1 when 2k₂a = nπ, a whole number of half-wavelengths of the inner wave. For these values the first is a = π/2k₂ = 0.56 nm: set a = 0.56 and the Physics panel reads 100.00%.
  • At E = U the sim uses T = 1/(1 + k₁²a²). For U = E = 0.30 eV and a = 0.50 nm, that is 33.7%.
See itSend the packet in at E = 0.60 eV. Watch for: a small reflected packet moving back to the left, and a Reflection estimate above zero.
07

A packet's outcome differs

The Physics panel gives T for one energy. A packet is a spread of energies, and each component meets the barrier with its own T. The packet's transmitted share is the average:

|φ(k)|² is the packet's distribution of wave numbers.
  • T rises steeply with E, so the higher-energy components gain more than the lower-energy ones lose. The average sits above the single-energy value: about 16% against 13.10% at the defaults.
  • A wider ΔE widens the gap. A narrower σ means a wider ΔE.
  • The transmitted part is made of the higher-energy components, so it leaves slightly faster than the incoming packet: about 0.29 against 0.265 nm/fs at the defaults.
  • The bar is an "estimate": it adds back the probability absorbed at the edges of the grid, and appears only after the packet has met the barrier.

08

Where it matters

  • Scanning tunneling microscope. The current through the vacuum gap between a sharp tip and a surface depends steeply on the gap. In this rectangular model with a 4 eV barrier, 0.1 nm more gap cuts T by a factor of about 8, which is why single atoms show up as bumps.
  • Alpha decay. Gamow explained it as an alpha particle tunneling through the barrier around the nucleus. Because T is so steep, half-lives range from under a microsecond to billions of years.
  • Flash memory. Charge is moved through a thin insulating oxide by tunneling, and the same effect is a leak in very thin transistor insulators.
T against half-width a: this sim's barrier (U − E = 0.10 eV) and a 4 eV vacuum gap.
09

Summary

In one line. A wave meeting a barrier is partly reflected and partly transmitted; for E < U the transmitted share falls roughly as e−4κa.

Key points

  • Where E < U the wave decays as e−κx; what reaches the far face keeps its original k.
  • T is steep in the thickness 2a and in U − E, through κ = √(2m(U − E))/ħ.
  • For E > U some wave still reflects; T = 1 only when 2k₂a = nπ.
  • A packet's outcome is T averaged over its energy spread.

Common mix-ups

  • "The particle borrows energy to climb the barrier." The transmitted wave has the same k, hence the same energy. The barrier removes amplitude, not energy.
  • "With E above U, everything gets through." Waves reflect wherever k changes, even above the barrier.
  • "The bar should match the Physics panel exactly." The panel is for one energy; the packet has a spread.

Things to try on your own

  • At U = 0.30 eV and E = 0.20 eV, find the smallest a (to 0.01 nm) where the Physics panel's T falls below 1%.
  • At E = 0.60 eV, sweep a and note where the Physics panel reads 100.00%. Compare with a = nπ/2k₂.
  • At the defaults, set σ to 0.50, 1.50 and 3.00 nm (with x₀ = −10 nm for the last) and record the Transmission estimate each time.
